curtain.name: Before | Now
curtain.help: Drag the curtain. Smooth water reflects the radar pulse away from the satellite and looks dark; rough surfaces look bright.

change.name: Change
change.help: Each pixel shows how much the signal changed between before and the chosen date. Raise the threshold to ignore small changes, such as rain on the ground.

classes.name: Classes
classes.help: The decision-tree result: new water (flood) separated from water that already existed, according to the JRC mask.

coherence.name: Coherence
coherence.help: Compares the signal phase in the two passes. Near 1, nothing changed; near 0, the surface changed. It helps confirm changes with similar brightness.

hero.lead: CassAAndra Alert turns what the NISAR radar measures on the ground into maps you can read and use: where water rose, where land dried out, where forest burned. Even under clouds and smoke.
hero.note: We separate what the radar measures from what we suppose. Every hypothesis comes with its evidence and how strong it is.

globe.label: Globe showing the Americas and four monitored hotspots: fire in California, flood on the coast of Peru, drought in the northern Amazon and flood at Guaíba Lake
globe.cassAlt: Cass, the mascot, holding a location pin over a map
globe.cardText: New water where there was farmland, measured in the latest pass.

lenses.title: Three lenses to read what changed on the ground
lenses.lead: Each lens turns on a map layer. Color never stands alone: every class has an icon and a name.

flood.text: New, smooth water sends little signal back to the radar. Where the river overflowed, the image goes dark.
flood.source: Measured with: NISAR GCOV, HH polarization

drought.text: Shrinking floodplains and reservoirs reflect signal again. The shore moves out over what was water.
drought.source: Measured with: NISAR GCOV and the JRC water mask

fire_deforestation.text: Without a canopy, the radar loses the echo from the trees. The scar shows even under smoke.
fire_deforestation.source: Measured with: NISAR GCOV, HV polarization

how.title: From satellite to alert in five steps
how.altBefore: Radar image from January 2026: the lake and a narrow river look dark
how.altNow: Radar image from November 12, 2026: the dark water area grew and covered the land around the lake
how.caption: Guaíba Lake, Brazil. On radar, smooth water sends little signal back and looks dark. Illustrative image.

search.title: Search
search.text: We find the NISAR passes before (early 2026) and now over each hotspot.

crop.title: Crop
crop.text: We download only the hotspot area, not the whole multi-GB file.

measure.title: Measurement
measure.text: We compute the change in signal (HH and HV), the coherence and the accumulated rain.

classify.title: Classification
classify.text: A decision tree labels each cell: flood, drought, fire, deformation or stable.

explain.title: Explanation
explain.text: Cass separates what was measured from the hypothesis about the cause, always with date and source.

radar.title: How the radar sees through clouds

lband.title: L-band: long waves
lband.text: NISAR's wave is about 24 cm long and goes through cloud, rain and smoke. It works day and night.

hv.title: HV polarization: the echo of trees
hv.text: The wave leaves horizontal and comes back vertical when it hits branches and leaves. If the forest disappears, that echo drops.

coherence.title: Coherence: what stays the same
coherence.text: We compare two passes. What did not change has high coherence; water, fire and construction bring it down.

brand.title: Two A's that together form an M
brand.story: We are Brazilian. In May 2024, we watched the Guaíba rise higher than ever recorded and Porto Alegre go under water. That is why it is the first place Cass watches. But radar has no borders: the same method measures fire in California and drought in southern Africa.
brand.symbol: The symbol is terrain, antenna and alert at once. The two A's are Ana and Aline; where they cross, the M of Mirian is born. Around them, the radar's orbit sweeps the planet.
brand.symbolAlt: CassAAndra Alert symbol: two A's that cross to form an M, inside a blue and orange orbit
brand.promise: it separates what it measured from what it supposes, shows date and source, and warns when a measurement is not reliable.

validation.title: How we validate
validation.lead: We compare the classifier's result, cell by cell, with independent reference data that the model does not use to decide. The metrics are precision and F1 per reference.

jrc.name: JRC Global Surface Water
jrc.how: New water must lie outside JRC permanent water; water that receded must have been water in JRC.

sentinel1.name: Copernicus Sentinel-1
sentinel1.checks: Flood in open areas, with C-band radar
sentinel1.how: The same flooded area seen by another radar, on a date close to the NISAR pass.

deter.name: DETER (INPE)
deter.how: INPE deforestation alerts in the same area, between the two passes.

firms.name: FIRMS (NASA)
firms.how: NASA heat spots on the dates between the before and now images.

cta.title: Radar has no borders
cta.text: From the Guaíba to California, from the Rio Negro to Borneo: the same method, anywhere NISAR passes.

footer.data: Data: NISAR (NASA and ISRO) via ASF, GPM IMERG and FIRMS (NASA), NOAA CPC (RONI), CHIRPS, Copernicus Sentinel-1 and 2, ESA WorldCover, JRC Global Surface Water, DETER/INPE, WorldPop, OpenStreetMap, Meteomatics and Open-Meteo. Basemap: OpenFreeMap and OpenStreetMap.
footer.ai: Open source on GitHub. Cass and the brand symbol are AI-generated images. The app's numbers are sample data until the pipeline publishes the real ones.
